primarySense: to limit or modify a statement to make it less absolute
otherSenses: to meet the requirements for something
etymologyNote: Medieval Latin qualificare 'to attribute a quality to'

nearSynonyms.difference: takes the statement back entirely; qualify only narrows it
admits a point; qualify adds limits to one's own claim

examples.text: The author later qualified her claim, saying the drug helped most patients but not those with heart conditions.
The general called the battle a qualified success: the town was captured, but at a far higher cost than planned.
Economists qualified their forecast, adding that growth would continue only if oil prices stayed low.

satPassage: In the first edition of his book, the economist claimed that free trade always benefits every nation. Later editions ____ this bold statement, adding that some industries and workers can be seriously harmed in the short term.
mnemonic: Think of adding a 'qualifier' word like 'usually' or 'some' to soften a claim.

primarySense: to restrain, stop, or hold back something
etymologyNote: from chess: 'check' threatens the king and halts his movement

nearSynonyms.difference: slows progress; check suggests restraining or holding in control
the common meaning — inspect, not restrain

examples.text: The Constitution's system of checks and balances was designed so that no single branch could seize too much power.
Vaccination checked the spread of smallpox until the disease was finally eradicated.
She checked her anger, biting back the sharp words she longed to say.

satPassage: When wolves were removed from the park, the deer population grew without limit and stripped the riverbanks of vegetation. Reintroducing the predators in 1995 ____ this growth, allowing willows and aspens to recover for the first time in decades.

primarySense: based on reliable reasoning or evidence; well-founded
etymologyNote: Old English gesund 'healthy, whole' — unrelated to sound meaning noise

nearSynonyms.difference: holds up under stress; sound means logically valid
only seems reasonable; sound actually is

examples.text: The experiment was sound: it had a control group, a large sample, and results that other labs repeated.
Saving a portion of every paycheck is sound financial advice, since it protects you against emergencies.
Washington's decision to retreat from New York proved sound, preserving his army to fight another day.

satPassage: Critics initially mocked the engineer's unusual design for the tower. Careful testing showed that her calculations were entirely reliable, however, and the structure—built on such well-founded principles—has survived three major earthquakes. Her reasoning, it turned out, had been ____ all along.

primarySense: serious and worrying; solemn in manner
etymologyNote: Latin gravis 'heavy, serious' — unrelated to grave meaning burial place

nearSynonyms.difference: general; grave suggests weight and potential danger
sincere; grave is solemn and heavy

examples.text: Doctors warned that the infection posed a grave threat, since no available antibiotic could stop it.
Ignoring the scouts' warnings was a grave mistake; the enemy attacked at dawn from exactly the direction they had reported.
The judge's grave expression silenced the courtroom before she said a word.

satPassage: The report's authors avoided dramatic language, but their conclusions were deeply serious. They warned that without immediate repairs, the dam could fail during the next major storm, placing thousands of residents in ____ danger.

primarySense: to stop or halt a process; (arresting) strikingly attention-grabbing
otherSenses: to take someone into police custody
etymologyNote: Old French arester 'to stop, stay'

nearSynonyms.difference: restrains; arrest brings to a full stop
the police meaning; not about halting processes

examples.text: The new drug can arrest the progress of the disease, though it cannot reverse damage already done.
Emergency reforms arrested the empire's economic decline for a few decades but could not prevent its collapse.
The portrait is arresting: the girl's direct, unblinking gaze stops visitors in their tracks.

satPassage: Conservationists had watched the bird's population shrink every year for three decades. A captive breeding program launched in 1987 finally ____ that decline, and numbers have slowly risen ever since.

primarySense: mastery or thorough knowledge of a skill or subject
etymologyNote: Latin commandare 'to entrust, order'

nearSynonyms.difference: basic acquaintance; command is mastery
the common meaning — an instruction

examples.text: Nabokov's command of English was remarkable, especially since it was not his first language.
Her command of five languages made the queen an unusually effective diplomat.
The student's command of statistics allowed her to spot the error that experienced researchers had missed.

satPassage: Raised in a household where three languages were spoken, the translator developed an extraordinary ____ of Spanish, Portuguese, and Italian, moving between them so easily that native speakers often assumed each was her first language.

primarySense: to rise in value over time
etymologyNote: Latin appretiare 'to set a price on' (pretium 'price')

nearSynonyms.difference: someone adds to it; appreciate is value rising on its own
the common meaning — gratitude

examples.text: Homes in the neighborhood appreciated rapidly, doubling in value within five years of the new train station.
Gold appreciated sharply during the war, as frightened investors fled from paper currency.
The painting he bought for a few dollars appreciated so much that his grandchildren sold it for millions.

satPassage: Many collectors bought rare comic books in the 1960s for less than a dollar each. Because so few copies survived in good condition, these comics ____ dramatically in the following decades, with some selling for over a million dollars.
mnemonic: apPRECIate ~ PRICE: its price goes up.

primarySense: careful, efficient use of resources or words; thrift
otherSenses: the system of production and trade in a region
etymologyNote: Greek oikonomia 'household management' (oikos 'house' + nomos 'law')

nearSynonyms.difference: thrift with money; economy also applies to words and motion
shortness; economy means nothing wasted

examples.text: Hemingway's economy of language—short sentences, few adjectives—makes every word carry weight.
Cheetahs hunt with great economy, saving their bursts of speed for the final seconds of a chase.
Lincoln's Gettysburg Address is famous for its economy: just 272 words that redefined the war.

satPassage: Haiku poets have only seventeen syllables in which to capture an image or emotion. This strict limit forces a remarkable ____ of expression: every unnecessary word must be cut, and each remaining one must do as much work as possible.

primarySense: to produce or provide a result; to give way under pressure
etymologyNote: Old English gieldan 'to pay, repay'

nearSynonyms.difference: admits defeat in an argument; yield can be physical or produce results
general; yield often implies a return on effort

examples.text: The experiment yielded surprising results: the plants grew faster in darkness than in light.
After a month-long siege, the city finally yielded to the invading army.
The new farming method yielded twice as much rice per acre as traditional planting.

satPassage: For years, the dig site produced nothing but broken pottery. Then, in its final season, careful excavation of a collapsed wall ____ an extraordinary find: a sealed jar containing dozens of perfectly preserved scrolls.

primarySense: specific and real rather than abstract or vague
etymologyNote: Latin concretus 'grown together, solid'

nearSynonyms.difference: stated clearly; concrete is specific and tangible
based on observation; concrete is real and specific

examples.text: Voters wanted concrete plans, not vague promises about 'a brighter future.'

satPassage: The candidate's speeches were full of grand themes like "renewal" and "opportunity," but they rarely included specific proposals. Voters increasingly demanded ____ details—how much each program would cost, who would run it, and when it would begin.

primarySense: done intentionally and with careful thought; (verb) to consider carefully
etymologyNote: Latin deliberare 'to weigh well' (libra 'scales')

nearSynonyms.difference: calm and restrained; deliberate stresses intention
the opposite: unintended

examples.text: The author's misspellings are deliberate, mimicking how the uneducated narrator would actually write.
The jury deliberated for three days, carefully reviewing every piece of evidence before reaching a verdict.
The general moved at a deliberate pace, refusing to rush his troops into an ambush.

satPassage: At first, viewers assumed that the gaps in the film's soundtrack were technical errors. The director later explained that every silence was intentional and carefully planned—a ____ choice meant to make the audience feel the characters' isolation.

primarySense: showing refined taste and good judgment in distinguishing quality
etymologyNote: Latin discriminare 'to divide, distinguish'

nearSynonyms.difference: wise in decisions; discriminating is refined in taste and perception

examples.text: A discriminating reader, she could tell within a page whether a novel was worth finishing.

The Medici were discriminating patrons, funding only artists whose talent they judged truly exceptional.

satPassage: The gallery owner rarely accepts new artists, rejecting hundreds of portfolios each year. Her eye for genuine talent is so refined that collectors treat her approval as a guarantee of quality, trusting her ____ judgment over that of most critics.

primarySense: to consider an idea or possibility seriously
etymologyNote: French entretenir 'to hold together, maintain'

nearSynonyms.difference: agrees with it; entertain merely considers it
the opposite: refuses to consider

examples.text: Most astronomers would not even entertain the idea that the continents moved until evidence from the seafloor forced them to.

satPassage: For centuries, physicians refused even to consider the possibility that invisible organisms might cause disease. Only after Louis Pasteur's experiments in the 1860s were most doctors willing to ____ the idea seriously.

primarySense: a large number of people or things
otherSenses: an organism that supports a parasite
etymologyNote: Latin hostis 'army' (this sense) — a different origin from host 'one who entertains'

nearSynonyms.difference: very close; multitude is more formal and often about people
the opposite: a small number

examples.text: Poor sleep is linked to a host of problems, including weaker memory, weight gain, and depression.
The new material has a host of possible uses, from bulletproof vests to lighter airplane wings.

satPassage: The move to a four-day school week was intended simply to save money on buses and heating. Instead, it brought a whole ____ of unexpected consequences, from childcare shortages to changes in students' test scores and sleep habits.

primarySense: restraint in expressing feelings or opinions
otherSenses: a supply kept for future use
etymologyNote: Latin reservare 'to keep back'

nearSynonyms.difference: unwillingness to speak; reserve is broader emotional restraint
cold distance; reserve can be polite and warm

examples.text: Beneath her cool reserve, the governess felt a passion she would never allow herself to show.
British soldiers were famous for their reserve, joking calmly even while under heavy fire.
In interviews, the usually reserved scientist spoke with surprising emotion about her late mentor.

satPassage: The queen was known for her emotional restraint, rarely smiling in public and never revealing her opinions on political matters. Biographers have debated whether this ____ reflected her true personality or was a role she believed her position required.

primarySense: to moderate or soften something by adding a balancing element
otherSenses: to harden metal by heating and cooling
etymologyNote: Latin temperare 'to mix in due proportion, restrain'

nearSynonyms.difference: reduces something harmful; temper balances or softens

examples.text: The company tempered its optimism, warning investors that sales might fall before they rose.

satPassage: The new findings about the cancer treatment are exciting, but the researchers urge caution. They ____ their enthusiasm by noting that the trial included only forty patients and that the long-term effects of the drug remain unknown.

etymologyNote: be- + Old French trair 'to hand over' (Latin tradere)

nearSynonyms.difference: argues for; champion fights for with personal energy

satPassage: When the young author's first manuscript was rejected by eleven publishers, one editor refused to give up on it. She defended the book in meetings, wrote letters to reviewers, and persuaded her company to print it, tirelessly ____ a novel that went on to win national awards.

primarySense: to lose energy or enthusiasm; to weaken
etymologyNote: possibly from obsolete flag 'hanging down, drooping'

nearSynonyms.difference: gradual decline of power or size; flag is about energy and enthusiasm

satPassage: The first months of the campaign drew enormous crowds and enthusiastic volunteers. By late autumn, however, public interest had begun to ____, and the candidate's rallies were attracting only a fraction of their earlier audiences.

primarySense: firmly fixed or attached; loyal and unwavering
etymologyNote: Old English fæst 'firm, secure' — the 'quick' meaning developed later

nearSynonyms.difference: describes persistent people; fast describes being firmly fixed

examples.text: Despite enormous pressure, the protesters held fast to their demands and refused to leave the square.

satPassage: During the storm, sailors lashed the cargo to the deck with heavy ropes. Although the ship rolled violently for hours, the crates remained ____, firmly secured in place, and not a single one was lost overboard.

examples.text: It is telling that the hero never mentions his father; the silence speaks louder than any description could.

satPassage: Before the new tutoring program, the school's reading scores had remained flat for a decade. In its first year, however, students showed a clearly noticeable rise, with scores jumping fifteen points—a ____ improvement that surprised even the program's designers.

examples.text: Martin Luther spoke with such conviction that he refused to recant even when threatened with death.

satPassage: Many reformers abandoned the campaign for women's suffrage after repeated defeats. Susan B. Anthony never did; her firm ____ that women deserved the vote sustained her through decades of setbacks, arrests, and public ridicule.

primarySense: to consider or think of someone or something in a particular way
etymologyNote: French regarder 'to look at'

nearSynonyms.difference: formal; implies a deliberate judgment

examples.text: Critics once regarded the novel as light entertainment; today it is regarded as a masterpiece.

satPassage: During her lifetime, Emily Dickinson was largely unknown, and the few critics who saw her poems considered them odd and unpolished. Today, however, she is widely ____ as one of the most original poets in the English language.
